record.paper_title: Underwater and Air-Water Wireless Communication: State-of-the-art, Channel Characteristics, Security, and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can machine-learning-based security methods that already appear promising in underwater communication, such as learning-based authentication or anti-eavesdropping approaches, be adapted and validated for air-water wireless communication systems?

evidence.quote: As security improvements provided by machine learning tools in underwater communication looks quite promising, we believe that experimenting on air-water communication will most likely yields equally interesting results.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication scenario in which signals must traverse both an aerial channel and an underwater channel, crossing the air–water interface (an "air–water" link). Such a link experiences combined impairments including atmospheric turbulence, refraction and Fresnel reflection at the interface, wave-induced surface roughness, absorption and scattering in the water column, and turbulence-induced fading in the aquatic medium. In purely underwater wireless communication, machine-learning-based security techniques (e.g., learning-based physical-layer authentication using channel features, and learning-based anti-eavesdropping schemes that exploit channel reciprocity or adversarial training) have shown promising performance.

Develop and rigorously validate machine-learning-based security methods—specifically (i) physical-layer authentication and (ii) anti-eavesdropping / secrecy-enhancing schemes—that are tailored to the combined air–water channel. A complete solution should:
1. Provide a tractable statistical or hybrid model of the air–water channel suitable as input/feature space for learning algorithms.
2. Define adversary models (spoofing transmitter and passive/active eavesdropper) at the air side, the water side, and at the interface.
3. Design learning algorithms (supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement-learning based) whose decision statistics exploit features unique to the air–water channel.
4. Provide theoretical guarantees (e.g., bounds on false-acceptance/false-rejection probabilities for authentication, or achievable secrecy rates for anti-eavesdropping) under the proposed channel model.
5. Validate the methods through simulation and/or experimental measurement and compare them against baselines designed for purely underwater or purely aerial links.

The problem is to determine whether such methods can match or exceed the security performance attained in the purely underwater setting.
artifact.category_tag: Machine-learning physical-layer security for air–water wireless channels
artifact.status_search_result: A brief literature check indicates that machine-learning-based physical-layer security (authentication and anti-eavesdropping) has been actively studied for underwater acoustic and optical channels, but adaptation and experimental validation specifically for cross-medium air–water links remains an emerging research direction with no comprehensive solution reported. The question is therefore treated as open.

status_evidence.claim: Adapting ML-based security to air–water links is identified as an open research direction.
